en: In the twelfth fascicle of the *Shi Dunlun Jizhuan Lunben* (The Collected Explanations of the Discourse Text by Shi Dunlun), within the section on "Mental Application and Its Objects," the third part follows, providing a general analysis. This section consists of seven parts. First:
The basis for the cultivation of mental attention;
second, the four conditions for entering meditative attainment;
third, the three ways of attaining concentration.
4. The distinctions among the four types of pure concentration (*śuddhaka-samādhi*); 5. The differences between the fourfold and fivefold concentrations;
6. Entering and emerging from them in sequential and non-sequential (leap-over) order.
Seventh is the distinction of repeated cultivation (*punarbhāvanā-viśeṣa*).
This refers to those very same various characteristics, up to and including their ability to perform the four functions and so forth.
Master Jìng’s commentary states:
That is to say, among the four characteristics— the characteristic of the object, the characteristic of causes and conditions,
and so forth— one attends to them with mental attention, which is capable of performing four functions;
the first is the cultivation of such mental attention itself.
Second, it can distance one from the remaining afflictions;
third, it can refine this mental attention as well as others, causing them to become increasingly bright and vigorous;
fourth, it brings about weariness toward the object of focus, preventing the afflictions from continuing.
Baso says: Furthermore, while practicing this mental attention (*manasikāra*), the repudiation of the object of focus is the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*);
the abandonment of all afflictions is the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*).
Maintaining the state of cessation is the path of liberation;
causing all afflictions to distance themselves from the continuum is the path of advancement.
One enters meditative attainment through four causal conditions.
As for the power of the cause (*hetubala*): this refers to the meditative absorption that was previously entered as the causal force for what is to be entered [in the present].
This theoretical analysis is formulated in accordance with the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) teachings.
In the Mahāyāna, the seeds of meditative concentration (*samādhi-bīja*) are taken as the causal force. Alternatively,
it may be based on the fact that when one previously entered a dhyāna in close proximity [to the present moment],
the function of the seeds of concentration was perfumed and increased, thereby giving rise to concentration at the present time.
This is due to the power of that cause.
Among those who have attained meditative concentration,
Bei (Bai) says:
These [afflictions] such as craving and so forth belong to the higher realms;
they do not pertain to the desire realm, because one enters meditative absorption only after having suppressed desire-attachment and the like.
This interpretation is incorrect.

According to the *Vijñānakāya-śāstra*, it is only for one who has attained the fundamental meditative absorption (*mauladhyāna*) of a particular stage that the afflictions (*kleśa*) of that stage may manifest.
How could it be possible for one who has not yet arisen in such absorption to first give rise to craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and other afflictions belonging to a higher stage?
Master Ki said:
"Regarding these four neutral roots (avyākṛta-mūla),
there are four types of persons who attain meditative concentration and give rise to these four kinds."
It is not necessarily the case that a single person must possess the capacity to give rise to all four [afflictions].
"Craving" (tṛṣṇā) refers to the mental factor of greed (lobha). "View" (dṛṣṭi) refers to the view of grasping at views (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa).
Pride is precisely the pride of "I" (asmimāna);
doubt is precisely deluded doubt.
Among these, [the latter] arises first upon hearing [the teaching].
These four faculties that arise prior to attaining meditative concentration are not exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*),
because they may also be unwholesome (*akuśala*) in the desire realm.
Alternatively, it is only those four types that arise after one has attained concentration which are indeterminate.
Commentary on the Vision:
It was stated above regarding meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) that one first gives rise to the view of eternalism based on false teachings;
subsequently, it was said that through such means, one enters the first *dhyāna* and so forth, thereby attaining purity and the like.
Furthermore, that teacher instructs that if one enters the eight meditative absorptions, there will be such things as permanence, self, purity, and liberation;
moreover, based on that teaching, one gives rise to the grasping of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
Relying on that view of permanence and the grasping of views, one applies oneself with vigor and diligence to enter the first dhyāna or other absorptions.
Furthermore, due to the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one perceives past events and again gives rise to the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*).
Next, it is explained that based on such views, one attains dhyāna through cultivation.
Subsequently, relying on the power of concentration, one knows past events and again gives rise to the view of eternalism.
Furthermore, at a later time, based on the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*), one further gives rise to the grasping of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
This is the interpretation of Ki.

Regarding the statement that "having thus entered [meditative absorption], one is able to recollect many past eons and subsequently gives rise to such views," this means that having attained concentration,
one gives rise to four types of eternalist views by taking the world as their general object.
It is not merely because it is conventionally designated as such that it is not subsumed under the higher dhyānas of the view-heap (*dṛṣṭi*).
Clinging to this view and refusing to relinquish it is called "clinging to views" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
However, in this passage, only the capacity to attain purity is mentioned, not the excellence of its essential nature (*svabhāva*).
It is difficult to explain in detail that [the view of self] is actually [a form of] grasping at what is difficult to manifest; rather, it is for the sake of ease.
Furthermore, since the aggregates are the basis for the common misconception of permanence, they are also the objects of the grasping at views.
In this context, craving takes the higher realms as its object; this has been fully explained according to the Vijñaptimātra system.
Prior to attaining meditative concentration, the conceit of "I" (asmimāna) arises taking these same realms as its object, and thus clings to them as being identical to itself.
This is because it can only arise by taking the five aggregates as its collective object.
Furthermore, the pride that arises after attaining meditative concentration likewise takes that same level as its object.
The conceit of self (*asmimāna*) does not arise with another stage as its object when lacking specific conditions;
however, this may be the case for that which takes [the aggregates] collectively as its object, as explained in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
Regarding the doubt concerning one dharma:
judging by the force of the textual context, this doubt regarding the Noble Truths arises only in those who cultivate supramundane [insight];
however, speaking from the perspective of what is predominant, the principle applies to other realms as well.
Because doubt also arises regarding other superior concentrations,
its nature prior to attaining concentration is generally unwholesome;
once concentration has been attained, it is termed an indeterminate root.
This concentration takes afflictions as its root to give rise to further afflictions.
Regarding the relish for this concentration, two meanings are explained:
first, it generally extends to the *anāgamya* (preliminary) stage.
Since the aforementioned *manasikāra* of signs (*nimitta*) pertains to both hearing and wisdom (*śruta-mayī* and *cintā-mayī*), it occurs even in the distracted mind of the *anāgamya* stage;
why, then, should it not also exist in a defiled (*kliṣṭa*) mind of that same stage?
It is only once one has attained the fundamental dhyāna (*mauladhyāna*) and achieved mastery over it that [the sign] arises manifest before the mind.
Second, it is said that one who has not yet reached the stages is free from defilement;

furthermore, one who has realized the characteristics [of the truths] is not yet fully endowed with the wisdom derived from hearing. Regarding those who relish what they love, it should be said that they have already emerged [from the desire realm], while those who are able to relish it should be said to be currently entering [the path].
Since it was previously stated that one who has attained meditative concentration (*samādhi*) immediately gives rise to relish (*āsvādana*),
there may be a suspicion that this relish arises while still within the pure concentration (*śuddha-samādhi*). Therefore,
it is now stated that the relished pure concentration has already been exited.
The mind capable of love should be said to have correctly entered [the meditative state]. Ji says:
"Pure concentration has already entered the past and emerged into the present."
Because the meditative absorption of taste exists in the present, it should be said that one is "correctly entering" it.
As for pure dhyāna, it can be cultivated and entered only by those with middling or sharp faculties who possess attenuated afflictive tendencies and subtle mental objects.
It does not say that those of inferior faculties, or those in whom the three poisons predominate, can attain pure concentration through cultivation;
rather, it is only by fixing the mind on and contemplating the realm of ambrosia in this manner that one enters the untainted concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*).

Whether it be the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths or the contemplation of the two kinds of emptiness, the True Suchness (tathatā) revealed thereby serves as the preliminary expedient for entering the untainted concentration (anāsrava-samādhi), which is termed the "Realm of Ambrosia" (amṛta-dhātu).

Regarding the concentration of the stage conducive to decline (hāna-bhāgīya-samādhi), this refers to those of dull faculties; the concentration of the stage conducive to maintenance (sthiti-bhāgīya-samādhi) refers to those of middling faculties or those of sharp faculties by nature.
In this context, the faculties are explained based on four individuals who each fulfill one of the four [categories];
it is not based on a single individual who possesses all four types.
This will be explained below in the thirteenth [chapter].
The *Catuḥparīkṣā-sūtra* states that one practices according to a sequence based on a single person;
logically, there are those of superior faculties who regress downward,
as well as those of inferior faculties who do not regress while progressing upward.
The concentration of the stage of decline (hāna-bhāgīya) declines;
the concentration of the stage of maintenance (sthiti-bhāgīya) enters into and emerges from defiled states of mind;
it neither progresses nor regresses.
The "concentration of the stage conducive to excellence" (anuloma-viśeṣa-bhāgīya-samādhi) refers to the cultivation of concentration by a specific individual;
this person possesses sharp faculties (tīkṣṇendriya).
It does not enter into or emerge from it together with a defiled mind;
the fourth [dhyāna] is likewise.
The concentration of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) is able to produce the untainted (*anāsrava*).
It is not the concentration of the superior portion (*viśeṣa-bhāgīya-samādhi*). This is stated in the thirteenth [sūtra],
the *Catuḥparīkṣā-caryā-sūtra*, where it is said that the concentration conforming to the superior portion is neither regressive nor stationary.
Because these are exclusively superior progressions and not the actual transition into the stage of penetration (*nirvedha*),
"penetration" (*nirvedha*) is used as a designation for the "stages leading to penetration" (*nirvedhabhāgīya*). This [term] has the sense of a "limb" (*aṅga*) or a "category" (*jāti*).
Regarding the phrase "just as worldly objects such as jeweled vases have already been well-sifted," this means that having already been sifted by the noble ones (ārya),
they enter into the most excellent portion, which is called the stage of penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya).
Just as a worldly jewel-vessel has already been selected and refined,
it is therefore called the "stage of selection" (*viveka-bhāgīya*).
These are the four types of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Briefly, it is distinguished by way of six gates.
First, the analysis of the modes of activity (*ākāra*), as in the text.
Second, the nature:
it is exclusively contaminated wholesome.
Third, the basis: the stages.
This applies to both the form and formless realms,
because even the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) can give rise to untainted (*anāsrava*) thought.

However, by inference from the meaning, this does not apply to the seven lower preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*), as they lack the fourth [dhyāna] and thus do not possess the mutual entry into and emergence from untainted thought.
What arises initially does not do so in the same manner as what arises subsequently;
therefore, all [conditioned phenomena] possess four parts, as there is no scriptural passage that negates this.
Of these four, the initial part is capable of producing two: itself and the abiding part.
The *sthiti-bhāgīya* (abiding portion) produces three, excluding the fourth;
the third (*viśeṣa-bhāgīya*) also produces three, excluding the *hāna-bhāgīya* (declining portion);
and the fourth (*nirvedha-bhāgīya*) produces one, namely its own kind.
Fifth, the distinction of categories:
the stage conducive to decline accords with the afflictions; the stage conducive to maintenance accords with its own level;
and the stage conducive to excellence accords with the higher levels.
The aids to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya) accord with the outflow-free (anāsrava).
Six arise based on [the dhyānas];
four arise from the lower realms.
In the two upper realms, there are only three [types of attainment] and not the first, because there is no falling back.
Within the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) of the immediate succession (*ānantarya*), all three types—defiled (*sāsrava*), undefiled (*anāsrava*), and mixed—each possess four categories.
First, purely impure; second, purely pure; third, a mixture of the pure and the impure.
Regarding the four types of entry:
first, entry in forward order; second, entry in reverse order; third, entry in both forward and reverse order; fourth, entry in both reverse and forward order.
Among these, there are only the first two.
Within the meditative attainments of "leap-over" entry (*vyutkrāntaka-samāpatti*),
each of the three types— contaminated (*sāsrava*), uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), and mixed (*miśra*)— likewise possesses four varieties.
Within this context, only the first two are distinguished because the wording applies universally.
Thus, there are twenty-four propositions in total.
The above has distinguished the categories.
As for the question of who is able to transcend them:
the term "transcend" (超) refers to this.

It pertains exclusively to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) and not to those still in training (*śaikṣa*); it pertains exclusively to those of sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*) and not to those of dull faculties (*mṛdvindriya*).
As for its realm, it pertains exclusively to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and not to the two higher realms.
Regarding this, Jingyun states:
"If one allows that a person in a lower stage can give rise to a wholesome mind born of the higher stages, twenty-four permutations can be established.
An ancient authority provides the proof as follows:
This follows the text on the "Vast Mind.
It means that from the mind of skillful means, one enters the non-obscured neutral mind because the emerging mind does not exert effort in seeking;
and the non-obscured neutral mind does not give rise to the wholesome mind of skillful means because it is weak and inferior.
Therefore, one enters the divine eye and ear consciousness from a mind in pure concentration;
however, the divine eye and ear consciousness cannot subsequently re-enter pure concentration.
If the body remains in the desire realm, one does not give rise to the wholesome states acquired through birth in the higher realms.
From which mind do the divine eye and ear emerge?
Furthermore, when an Arhat of the desire realm falls back and gives rise to the afflictions of the two higher realms,
if he does not give rise to the innate wholesome mind of those higher realms, from what kind of mind does he enter into those afflictions?
Furthermore, when an Arhat enters a meditative absorption that transcends [the realm of nothingness],
if he does not attain the wholesome mind acquired at birth within the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana), the enumeration of the factors would be incomplete.
Now, according to the texts of the Abhidharma within the Mahāyāna:
It is said that one attains the wholesome mind of maturation belonging to whichever level one is born into;
this is designated as "maturation" based on its arising in the present.
This passage explains that although the body resides in a lower level, one gives rise only to the wholesome mind of innate acquisition (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala-citta*) belonging to that lower level.
Regarding the three proofs prior to the assembly:

according to various newly translated sūtras and śāstras, both the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇacitta*) are termed "fruits of supernormal power" (*abhijñā-phala*).
The *Nyāyānusāra* and other treatises all make this same determination.
Just as when cultivating the supernormal powers (abhijñā), one unimpededly severs all obstructions until they are completely cleared away,
next one brings to maturity the wisdom of the mental ground (manobhūmi);
this constitutes the essence of those supernormal powers.
From this, the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇacitta*) arise; these are all termed "fruits of supernormal power" (*abhijñā-phala*).
Because they enter into and emerge from meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the divine eye and divine ear emerge from concentration and likewise re-enter it.
Furthermore, when a person beyond training (aśaikṣa) falls back and gives rise to afflictions of a higher stage,
they arise from the abiding portion of meditative concentration (*sthiti-bhāgīya-samādhi*) as afflictions of that same stage.
This is just as when one guards against the faults of a higher stage, one may enter the pure abiding portion of concentration of a lower stage by means of the afflictions of the higher stage.
When one who has attained the state beyond training (aśaikṣa) regresses, they enter into afflictions from the stage of non-regression (aparihāṇabhāga) into the stage of stability (sthitibhāga).
Once it is known that, having been born in a lower realm, one gives rise to the innate wholesome mind (upapattilābhika-kuśalacitta) of a higher stage,
then when entering the eight meditative attainments (dhyāna) in both direct and reverse order, skipping over stages, multiple sequential phrases would not be established.
There are six categories in total:
first, entering the eight meditative absorptions (dhyāna) through both the forward and reverse sequences of the contaminated (sāsrava);
second, entering the seven meditative absorptions through both the forward and reverse sequences of the uncontaminated (anāsrava).
1. Entering the eight meditative absorptions (dhyāna) through the contaminated states (*sāsrava*) by way of both forward and reverse order and by skipping every other stage;
2. Entering the eight meditative absorptions through the contaminated states by way of both forward and reverse order and by skipping every other stage;
3. Entering the seven meditative absorptions through the uncontaminated states (*anāsrava*) by way of both forward and reverse order and by skipping every other stage.
When entering the eight meditative attainments through the six outflows and the outflow-free states by way of direct, reverse, or alternating sequences,
if one emerges from a mind that has transcended the form realm, there may be a mind born of hearing, a mind born of maturation, or a mind resulting from supernormal power.
Now, from which mind does one emerge when emerging from the mind of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?

It emerges from the innate wholesome mind (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala-citta*) that arises in a different stage, rather than from the minds of hearing-wisdom (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*), deportment (*airyāpathika*), craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), or the fruit of supernormal powers (*abhijñā-phala*).
The mind born of maturation (*vipākaja*), being the fruit of karma, does not arise in a stage different from its own.

By analogy with the emergence from the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), it is accepted that [this mind] takes three kinds of objects and contacts three kinds of contacts, arising in dependence upon internal and external conditioned aggregates (*saṃskṛtasaṃghāta*).
What prevents a mind born of maturation (*vipākaja*) belonging to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) from arising in the Desire Realm, provided it is not the fruit of karma?
However, its characteristics are difficult to discern.

For this reason, one should say that a "mind of emergence" (*vyutthāna-citta*) refers to that which emerges into a different category—whether it be contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*)—and does not necessarily require a state of distraction.
If that is so, how can one abide in a different category when entering into a mixture of contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) states?
Now, it is said that "emerging" (*vyutthāna*) refers to abiding in a distinct category with a different mode of activity (*ākāra*).
Alternatively, there is no contradiction in principle if one gives rise to an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) mind.
Because it is extremely distant, no one is able to leap over to the third meditative attainment (samāpatti), with the sole exception of the Tathāgatas and others;
this statement is made in reference to those who possess the mastery to leap across all stages (bhūmi).
If those from the seventh stage and below, as well as śrāvakas who practice the pāramitās, are also able to transcend up to the seventh stage—
just as Mahāmaudgalyāyana entered the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness and yet heard the sounds of elephants and other such things.
This is because one emerges from that state by transcending the various stages (*bhūmi*).
This matter is explained in full within the sixty-third [chapter].
Furthermore, it relies on mastery to transcend all stages.
This refers to Buddhas and non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas;
although other persons may transcend [the dhyānas], they cannot do so extensively.
If one transcends the dhyānas spontaneously, all such persons attain this.
This is because [the Buddha] was like one who has been reborn in the nine stages, as well as Mahāmaudgalyāyana;
therefore, this is not mentioned among the cultivated [powers].
The text has two parts:
first, it clarifies the mixed cultivation of the two meanings;
second, it clarifies the distinctions between cultivated birth.
There are five categories of perfuming (*vāsanā*).
First is the cultivation through purely impure meditative concentration (*samādhi*),
which refers to being born in the lower four dhyānas, excluding the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*).
As explained below, by cultivating [the concentrations] in the weak, medium, and superior grades, one experiences the fruits of three stages.
Second is the perfuming of purely untainted concentration;
this refers to the exhaustion of tainted concentration within the death-and-rebirth of transformation (nirmāṇa-cyuti) from the eighth stage onward.
The three types of mixed cultivation— defiled, undefiled, and mixed—
are taught here for the sake of attaining mastery over the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and for experiencing the fruits of mastery over those attainments;
by practicing them in alternation, one is born in the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*) and so forth.
Fourth, the cultivation of the mixed determinate and indeterminate states with outflows (*sāsrava*),
which refers to an Arhat relinquishing meritorious actions that sustain life and the fruits of such merit.
Fifth, the cultivation of the mixed determinate and indeterminate states without outflows (*anāsrava*).
This refers to the death-and-rebirth through transformation (*pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa*) of the two vehicles and of Bodhisattvas prior to the seventh stage.
Within this third type of mixed cultivation,
the tainted (*sāsrava*) states constitute the two boundaries.
When a single moment of the untainted [state] occurs therein,
it is called "the completion of cultivation," just as the karma of the five Pure Abodes is produced by the bodies of ordinary beings.
The seeds planted within the body spontaneously serve only to extinguish rebirth in the lower celestial realms;

however, through the fulfillment of cultivation based on the arousal of aspiration, they empower the seeds of past karma with uncontaminated meditative concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*), causing their force to become so preeminent that one is born in the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*).
Therefore, it is not the case that they are contaminated (sāsrava) while serving as the middle [dhyāna].
Because their power is inferior,
this differs from the mixed cultivation (vyavakīrṇa-bhāvanā) of the Śrāvakas.
That is to say, the Abhidharma and other texts state that one first gives rise to the sixteen aspects of the untainted (*anāsrava*) contemplation, which continues in a succession of many moments;
subsequently, one enters the sixteen aspects of the tainted (*sāsrava*) contemplation, which likewise continues in a succession of many moments.

In this manner, through successive reduction of the objects of practice, until only two moments—each consisting of one uncontaminated and one contaminated moment—remain, the preparatory stage (prayoga) is perfected.
Immediately thereafter, one further arouses a single moment of the uncontaminated [path].
Furthermore, one more moment of contaminated [consciousness] arises;
this is the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*).
Immediately thereafter, one more moment of uncontaminated [consciousness] arises; this is the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
The name perfumes [the seeds] to form five grades.
Regarding the three minds of cultivation through perfuming,
this is because one uses the outflow-free (anāsrava) states at both ends to perfume the outflowing (sāsrava) state in the middle.
Furthermore, the first moment of contaminated [consciousness] is the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), which suppresses and removes the obstacles to meditative concentration (*samādhi-āvaraṇa*).
The subsequent moment of uncontaminated [consciousness] serves as the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*), which directly eliminates the obstacles to meditative concentration.
The next moment of contaminated [consciousness] constitutes the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), whereby the cultivation is brought to completion.
If one takes the contaminated (sāsrava) as the middle and the uncontaminated (anāsrava) as the beginning and end,
how could it be that the uncontaminated serves as the preparatory path (prayoga-mārga) and the contaminated as the path of immediate succession (ānantarya-mārga)? Furthermore,
since the final liberation at the end is that which provides the support, the supported and the support must be mutually compatible.
This refers to one who has already attained both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) four dhyānas and so forth. Generally,
for one who perfumes the meditative concentration,
it is necessary to fully possess all four types of dhyāna— both contaminated and uncontaminated— before one can begin the process of perfuming.
First, one uses the untainted (anāsrava) state of the fourth dhyāna to permeate the tainted (sāsrava) states of its own level;
next, one enters the untainted state of the third dhyāna to permeate the tainted states of its own level,
continuing in this manner down to the first dhyāna.
It is so called because [the influence] flows from the upper stream and infuses into the lower stage.
According to the subsequent text, there are five types of perfuming of meditative concentration (*samādhi*):
first, for the sake of attaining mastery over meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
Second, it is for the sake of attaining mastery over meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and dwelling in happiness in the present life;
third, it is for the sake of attaining the path from which there is no falling back;
fourth, it is for the sake of cultivating and purifying the path that leads to the acquisition of qualities (*guṇa*).
The fifth is for the sake of being born in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens;
in this present passage, only the first two are briefly mentioned.
If one wishes to enter various meditative absorptions (samādhi) at this place, at this time, and regarding this matter, [one should apply the appropriate resolve].
Tài says: "The body upon which one relies is called the 'basis' (*āśraya*), and so forth. Jī says:
"The basis upon which the body dwells is called the 'basis' (*sthāna*)."
The arising of meditative absorption, light, darkness, and so forth, as well as the seasons and such, are called "time.
Whatever object it conditions is called a "thing" (*vastu*).
If there were any other grasping, [it would be as follows].
If one who possesses residual karma for rebirth moistened by the link of grasping (*upādāna*) should pass away,
they will be born in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens.
The fruits of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) are twofold:
first, the fruit of acquired merit; second, the fruit of rebirth in the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*).
Within the distinctions of cultivation and birth, there are four types.
1. The cause of a lifetime;
2. the regression from defilement and the progress toward goodness;
3. the locus for cultivating the causes.
Fourth, the distinction:
Once one has been born there, if one gives rise to attachment to its flavor, one will then fall away;
however, it is not the case that there can be falling away from the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) of the higher stages.
Due to the excessive attachment to sensual flavors, their lifespan is diminished and their names vanish;
this is what is meant by "receding and being reborn.
In the extensive analysis of the five gates of this stage, the first three sections have already been explained, and the fourth gate is now concluded.
The fourth section below explains the essential tenets of various sūtras and,
finally, miscellaneous meanings.
The text is divided into two parts.
First, the essential points of the doctrine are explained;
that is, the interpretation of the four general headings previously mentioned,
specifically the latter three among the categories of dhyāna, vimokṣa, samādhi, and samāpatti.
Since the four dhyānas have already been explained previously,
the thirteenth fascicle explains the *Saṃyuktārthasūtra* only at this later point;

Answer: Because this [emptiness] contemplates existence, it is designated as that "mind."
Because he contemplates emptiness, all [phenomena] are simultaneously dispensed with.

The text is divided into three parts:

Regarding the phrase "because the two aspects of opposition and conformity are not associated":
when the mind takes an adverse object as its condition, it becomes dejected.
When the mind is uplifted by encountering favorable conditions, it is called "high.
Now, being free from these two characteristics is called "neither high nor low.
Furthermore, to be ruined regarding conventional truth and to oppose the mundane realm is called "low."
To maintain the mind and establish it in accordance with the true realm is called "elevated" (*āṅga*).
To practice the signless (*animitta*) and remain free from duality is called "neither elevated nor depressed" (*an-unnata-an-anata*).
This non-destruction of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*)—namely, not conceptualizing any signs, neither being weary of them nor destroying them—is called "not depressed."
Because one correctly contemplates this signless realm, one does not conform to stubborn attachment; thus it is called "not haughty.

Thereafter, he again repeatedly exhorts and encourages himself; this explains the fruit of the means (*upāya*).
"Characteristics" (*nimitta*) refers to objective signs; these have two levels:
first, those with outflows (*sāsrava*) are called "characteristics," while those without outflows (*anāsrava*) are called "signless" (*animitta*).
The conditioned is termed "with signs" (*sanimitta*) and the unconditioned is termed "signless" (*animitta*).

According to the first interpretation, all subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) takes as its objective essence either the latter meaning alone or both the latter and the former meanings; thus it is called "signless practice" (*animitta-caryā*).
This immediately extinguishes the four modes of activity (*ākāra*), or the four modes of the Path (*mārga*).
According to the latter interpretation, non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) is termed "practice without signs" (*animitta-caryā*).
The opposite of these two is called "practice with signs" (*sanimitta-caryā*).
Within this skillful means, those who have not yet attained liberation from those various signs remain in the state of outflows (*sāsrava*),
because they have not yet been liberated from the signs of outflows.
Therefore, the various secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*) disturb the mind from time to time;
only through repeated analytical discernment can one attain the fruit of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
Liberation from all outflowing secondary characteristics is termed the fruit of skillful means (*upāya-phala*).
Because one is well-liberated within this liberation, abiding spontaneously is called "ultimate liberation.
This pertains to both the fundamental and subsequent stages of wisdom (*mūla-prsthalabdha-jñāna*).
It is included within the categories of "clearly understanding the fruit" and "clearly understanding qualities."
The abandonment of afflictions and the truth of cessation are called the fruit of thorough understanding;
dwelling in happiness in the present life and the truth of the path are called the qualities of thorough understanding—
namely, that which is thoroughly understood through signless practice.
This refers to the four practices, which are also practice without marks (*animitta*).
There is a difference in breadth and narrowness between these two preceding and following passages. Jing says:
Regarding "the abandonment and the ultimate abiding," this is explained in terms of the essence of the two truths;
both are designated as "fruits" and "virtues."
Furthermore, from the section on Cessation and the Path onwards,
the sūtra text is explained by way of its application.
Moreover, the "clear realization of the truths" (satyābhisamaya) is a name for the path of seeing (darśanamārga).

If, in this place, those things and so forth do not exist—
this second stage is the distinct aspect of the practice of samādhi wherein the objects are identical;

Regarding the question, "Why is emptiness and so forth explained first here?"—
this third section explains the sequence of the three [truths].
The intent of this inquiry is to ask why, among the four aspects of suffering, impermanence and suffering are explained first.
Later, emptiness and selflessness will be explained.
Now, within this context, the practice of emptiness is explained first;
subsequently, the practice of wishlessness will be explained, followed by impermanence and the other [aspects].
This intention answers that there is no contradiction.
Regarding the "impermanence" among the sixteen aspects,
it refers to first observing impermanence when initially practicing the preparatory application prior to the Path of Seeing.
Because it is impermanent, it is suffering; because it is suffering, it is non-self.
Because it is non-self, it is empty.
This sequence is established by proceeding from the easy to the difficult.
In this context, because one first perceives that there is no person or phenomena when initially entering the path of seeing to contemplate suchness, emptiness is taught first.
From the true path of seeing, one then enters the path of seeing with signs.
Next, one must give rise to the contemplation of impermanence and suffering within the wishless state before purity can be attained.
To say that "if there were no contemplation of non-self, impermanence, and suffering, one would never attain purity" is an explanation by way of contrapositive reasoning.
If there were no concentration on selflessness and emptiness within the Path of True Seeing (*darśanamārga*),

this means that prior to the path of practice regarding impermanence within the stage of the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*),

wishing only for the signless, one is single-mindedly intent on seeking liberation.
